items.name: find-skills
items.author: vercel-labs
items.description: So their agent can intelligently recommend and install the right modular skills from the open ecosystem when they ask how to do something.
items.summary: Find Skills is a Vercel Labs agent skill that helps developers discover and install capabilities from the open agent skills ecosystem instead of reinventing workflows from scratch. When a user asks how to do something, whether a skill exists, or wants to extend agent capabilities, the skill routes through a six-step discovery flow: understand the domain and task, check the skills.sh leaderboard for proven options, search with `npx skills find`, verify install counts and source reputation, present install commands with skills.sh links, and optionally install via `npx skills add`. The Skills CLI acts as the package manager for modular skill packages that extend agents with specialized knowledge and workflows. Quality gates prefer skills with 1K+ installs, trusted sources like vercel-labs and anthropics, and repositories with meaningful GitHub stars. If nothing matches, the skill acknowledges the gap and can suggest `npx skills init` for a custom package.
highlights: Searches skills.sh and the Skills CLI with `npx skills find [query]`
Checks the skills.sh leaderboard before keyword search for proven skills
Verifies install counts, source reputation, and GitHub stars before recommending
Installs chosen packages with `npx skills add` including global `-g -y` flags
Covers web dev, testing, DevOps, docs, code quality, design, and productivity domains

items.name: grill-me
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Have an agent relentlessly pressure-test their plan or design until every decision branch is resolved and shared understanding is reached.
items.summary: grill-me is a user-invoked entry point that runs the repo's grilling session: the agent interviews the developer relentlessly about every aspect of a plan or design until both reach a shared understanding. Questions come one at a time, each with the agent's recommended answer, and the agent waits for feedback before continuing. Facts that can be found by exploring the codebase are looked up rather than asked; decisions are always put to the developer. The agent does not enact the plan until the developer confirms shared understanding. Developers reach for it before implementing anything non-trivial, to surface unexamined assumptions while they are still cheap to fix.
highlights: User-invoked slash command whose entire body is: run a /grilling session
The session asks questions one at a time, each with a recommended answer, waiting for feedback before continuing
Facts are looked up in the codebase; only genuine decisions are put to the user
The plan is not enacted until the user confirms shared understanding

items.name: grill-with-docs
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Pressure-test architecture decisions against their live codebase and living documentation before writing production code.
items.summary: grill-with-docs runs a relentless interview (a /grilling session) to sharpen a plan or design, and leaves a paper trail as it goes: it drives the /domain-modeling skill so resolved terminology lands in CONTEXT.md and hard-to-reverse decisions become ADRs. It is the stateful variant of the repo's grilling primitive, meant for when you have a codebase whose documented language the plan should be tested against; /grill-me is the stateless alternative when no repo exists. In the repo's main idea-to-ship flow it is the recommended starting point, before spec and ticket writing. Reach for it to stress-test an idea against your project's existing vocabulary and documented decisions while keeping those docs current.
highlights: Runs the repo's /grilling interview primitive against your plan or design
Drives the /domain-modeling skill so resolved terminology lands in CONTEXT.md and hard decisions become ADRs
Stateful counterpart to /grill-me: it retains what it learns in the repo's docs, leaving a paper trail
Recommended first step of the repo's idea-to-ship flow when a codebase exists

items.name: improve-codebase-architecture
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Safely deepen clusters of shallow modules into cohesive, testable units while respecting their external dependencies.
items.summary: improve-codebase-architecture surfaces architectural friction and proposes deepening opportunities: refactors that turn shallow modules into deep ones, aiming at testability and AI-navigability. It first reads CONTEXT.md and ADRs, then explores the codebase with an Explore subagent, applying the deletion test to suspected shallow modules. Findings are rendered as a self-contained HTML report in the OS temp directory using Tailwind and Mermaid, with one card per candidate covering files, problem, solution, benefits, before/after diagrams, and a recommendation-strength badge, ending with a top recommendation. It deliberately proposes no interfaces at this stage; once the user picks a candidate it runs the /grilling skill to walk the design, updating CONTEXT.md and offering ADRs for load-bearing rejections along the way. Developers reach for it when a codebase feels hard to navigate or test and they want ranked, visual refactor candidates instead of vague advice.
highlights: Explores the codebase via an Explore subagent, applying the deletion test to suspected shallow modules
Writes a self-contained HTML report to the OS temp directory with Tailwind and Mermaid via CDN
Each candidate card has files, problem, solution, benefits, before/after diagrams, and a Strong / Worth exploring / Spec
Uses the /codebase-design vocabulary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) exactly
After the user picks a candidate, runs the /grilling skill and updates CONTEXT.md and ADRs as decisions crystallize

items.name: frontend-design
items.author: anthropics
items.description: Generate distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces and components that avoid generic AI aesthetics.
items.summary: Frontend Design is Anthropic's agent skill for creating memorable, production-grade web interfaces that deliberately avoid generic AI aesthetics. Before any code ships, the skill forces a bold aesthetic direction: purpose, tone, constraints, and a single unforgettable differentiation point. Implementation covers working HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, or Vue with meticulous attention to typography pairings, cohesive color systems, high-impact motion, asymmetric spatial composition, and atmospheric backgrounds. It explicitly rejects overused fonts like Inter and Arial, purple-on-white gradient clichés, and cookie-cutter layouts that lack context-specific character. Maximalist visions receive elaborate animation and effects, while minimalist directions demand restraint and precision in spacing and detail. Developers reach for it when building landing pages, dashboards, React components, posters, or any web surface that must look intentionally designed rather than templated by default agent output patterns.
highlights: Commits to a bold aesthetic direction before writing any UI code
Covers typography, color systems, motion, spatial composition, and atmospheric backgrounds
Produces working code in HTML, CSS, JS, React, Vue, and related web stacks
Explicitly bans generic AI slop fonts, palettes, and predictable layouts
Scales implementation complexity to match maximalist or minimalist design visions

items.name: tdd
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Follow test-driven development with a strict red-green-refactor loop when creating reliable features or fixing bugs.
items.summary: tdd is a reference skill for running the red-green test-driven development loop inside Claude Code. It defines what a good test is (behavior verified through public interfaces, readable as a specification), introduces seams - the public boundaries tests live at - and requires those seams to be agreed with the user before any test is written. It names three anti-patterns to avoid: implementation-coupled tests, tautological assertions that recompute the expected value the way the code does, and horizontal slicing (writing all tests before any implementation). The loop rules are red before green, one vertical slice per cycle, and refactoring deferred to the review stage. Developers reach for it when building features or fixing bugs test-first, or when they want integration tests that survive refactors.
highlights: Defines good tests as behavior checks at public interfaces that read like specifications and survive refactors
Requires the seams under test to be written down and confirmed with the user before any test is written
Names 3 anti-patterns: implementation-coupled tests, tautological assertions, and horizontal slicing
Loop rules: red before green, one seam/test/implementation per cycle, refactoring deferred to the review stage
Reads CONTEXT.md (if present) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language

items.name: setup-matt-pocock-skills
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Scaffold the per-repo configuration that Matt Pocock’s engineering agent skills rely on so they understand the issue tracker, triage labels, and domain documentation la
items.summary: setup-matt-pocock-skills scaffolds the per-repo configuration that the repo's other engineering skills assume: where issues live, the triage label vocabulary, and the domain-doc layout. It is prompt-driven, not a script: it explores the repo (git remotes, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, CONTEXT.md, docs/adr/, .scratch/, monorepo signals), presents findings, and walks three sections with recommended defaults. Section A records the issue tracker (GitHub via gh, GitLab via glab, local markdown, or freeform other) in docs/agents/issue-tracker.md; Section B confirms the five canonical triage labels and only runs if the triage skill is installed; Section C defaults to single-context domain docs. After user confirmation it writes docs/agents/*.md from seed templates and adds an Agent skills block to whichever of CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md already exists. Run once before first use of the other engineering skills; later edits go straight into docs/agents/*.md.
highlights: Explores the repo first: git remotes, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, CONTEXT.md, docs/adr/, .scratch/, monorepo signals
Section A picks the issue tracker: GitHub (gh CLI), GitLab (glab CLI), local markdown under .scratch/, or a freeform 'ot
Section B keeps or overrides the 5 canonical triage labels; skipped entirely if the triage skill is not installed

items.name: handoff
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Compress long agent conversations into a clean, focused handoff document that lets the next agent pick up exactly where the previous one left off.
items.summary: handoff compacts the current conversation into a handoff document that a fresh agent can pick up to continue the work. The document is saved to the OS temporary directory rather than the workspace, includes a 'suggested skills' section for the next agent, and references existing artifacts (specs, plans, ADRs, issues, commits, diffs) by path or URL instead of duplicating their content. If the developer passes an argument, it is treated as a description of what the next session will focus on and the document is tailored accordingly. Developers reach for it when a session is ending, context is filling up, or work needs to move to another agent.

Includes a 'suggested skills' section telling the next agent which skills to invoke

items.name: triage
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Move issues and external PRs through a state machine of triage roles: categorise, verify claims against the codebase, grill if needed, and write agent-ready briefs.
items.summary: triage moves issues and external pull requests on the project tracker through a small state machine of roles: bug or enhancement as category, and needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-agent, ready-for-human, or wontfix as state. Invoked as /triage with a natural-language request, it can surface what needs attention in three buckets (unlabeled, needs-triage, needs-info with reporter activity), or triage a specific item: gather full context, check the codebase for existing implementations and .out-of-scope/ for prior rejections, recommend a category and state, verify the claim by reproducing the bug or running the PR's tests, grill the request into shape if needed, then apply the outcome - an agent brief for ready-for-agent, triage notes for needs-info, or a documented wontfix. Every comment it posts starts with an AI-generated disclaimer. Developers reach for it to run maintainer triage over a team or open-source backlog.
highlights: State machine with 2 category roles (bug, enhancement) and 5 state roles (needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-agent, rea
Treats an external PR as an issue with attached code - same roles, same states, same machine
Verifies claims before grilling: reproduces bugs from reporter steps, checks out PR diffs and runs tests
Checks for redundancy (already implemented) and prior rejection (.out-of-scope/) before recommending
Every comment posted to the tracker starts with a mandatory AI-generated triage disclaimer

items.name: prototype
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Quickly test business logic, state transitions, or data models interactively before committing to full implementation.
items.summary: prototype builds throwaway code that answers a single design question, and the question decides the shape. For 'does this logic or state model feel right?' it builds a tiny interactive terminal app that pushes the state machine through cases hard to reason about on paper; for 'what should this look like?' it generates several radically different UI variations on one route, switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar. Shared rules: the code is clearly marked throwaway, runs with one command, holds state in memory with no persistence, skips tests and abstractions, and surfaces the full relevant state after every action or variant switch. When done, the validated decision is folded into the real code and the prototype is committed to a throwaway branch with a pointer left on the implementation issue. Developers reach for it to settle a design question cheaply before building for real.
highlights: Two branches: logic questions get a tiny interactive terminal app, UI questions get radically different variations on on
UI variants are switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar
No persistence by default; state lives in memory, since persistence is what the prototype is checking
Skips polish: no tests, no abstractions, only enough error handling to stay runnable
When done, the validated decision goes into real code and the prototype is committed to a throwaway branch as a primary

items.name: grilling
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design, one question at a time, until shared understanding is reached.
items.summary: grilling is the model-invoked interview skill behind grill-me. The agent interrogates the developer about every aspect of a plan or design, walking down each branch of the design tree and resolving dependencies between decisions one-by-one, with a recommended answer attached to each question. Questions are asked one at a time, waiting for feedback before continuing, because multiple questions at once are bewildering. Facts that can be found by exploring the codebase are looked up instead of asked; decisions are always the developer's. The plan is not enacted until the developer confirms shared understanding. It fires when the developer wants to stress-test a plan before building or uses a 'grill' trigger phrase.
highlights: Interviews the developer about every aspect of the plan until shared understanding is reached

items.name: teach
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Maintain a precise, opinionated glossary that records mastered concepts with tight definitions and forbidden synonyms.
items.summary: teach turns the current directory into a stateful teaching workspace for learning a topic over multiple sessions. State lives in named files: MISSION.md captures why the user wants to learn, RESOURCES.md tracks high-trust sources, learning records capture insights like ADRs, and lessons are self-contained HTML files built from reusable components in ./assets. The philosophy splits learning into knowledge (from trusted resources, never parametric memory), skills (interactive lessons with tight feedback loops), and wisdom (delegated to real communities). Lessons are kept short, cited, tied to the mission, and aimed at the learner's zone of proximal development, with retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving used to build long-term retention. Developers reach for it when they want structured, multi-session learning of a new technology or concept rather than one-off answers.
highlights: Stateful workspace of named files: MISSION.md, RESOURCES.md, learning records, lessons, reference docs, assets, NOTES.md

Delegates wisdom questions to real communities such as forums, subreddits, or local groups

Agents must preserve identity continuity: meeting_id discovered under user identity stays on --as user; bot-joined meetings stay on --as bot. The skill enforces that +meeting-join is a visible write action requiring explicit user intent and a 9-digit meeting number, not a meeting link. For live summaries, +meeting-events must use --page-all by default and refresh before answering ongoing meeting content. It documents VC Agent beta scope errors, gray-list handling, and application identity permission checks. Cross-stage workflows chain to lark-vc for ended meetings and lark-im for posting results to groups. Use when users want a bot to join, monitor speakers, screen share, or chat in an active Lark meeting.

items.name: domain-modeling
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model: pin down domain terminology in a glossary and record architectural decisions as ADRs.
items.summary: domain-modeling is the active discipline of building and sharpening a project's domain model during design sessions. It challenges terms that conflict with the CONTEXT.md glossary, sharpens fuzzy or overloaded words (does 'account' mean the Customer or the User), stress-tests relationships with concrete edge-case scenarios, and cross-references stated behaviour against the code. Resolved terms are written to CONTEXT.md immediately rather than batched, and CONTEXT.md stays a pure glossary with no implementation details. ADRs are offered only when a decision is hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off. It supports single-context repos and multi-context repos via CONTEXT-MAP.md, creating files lazily only when there is something to write.
highlights: Challenges terms against the existing CONTEXT.md glossary the moment a conflict appears
Sharpens fuzzy or overloaded words by proposing a precise canonical term (does 'account' mean Customer or User)
Stress-tests domain relationships with invented edge-case scenarios and cross-references claims against the code
Updates CONTEXT.md inline as terms resolve, never batched; the file stays a pure glossary with no implementation details
Offers ADRs only when a decision is hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off

It spans dataset preparation, validation, training job submission, monitoring, grader calibration, deployment, evaluation, and cleanup across quickstart, full pipeline, dataset creation, iterative training, and diagnose-poor-results workflows. Bundled Python scripts cover submit_training, monitor_training, calibrate_grader, check_training curves, deploy_model via ARM REST, evaluate_model with an LLM judge, convert_dataset formats, generate distillation data, score_dataset quality, and cleanup resources. Five rules insist on baseline evaluation first, validated data before submit, RFT grader calibration targeting 25-50% base-model failure, checkpoint evaluation before deploy, and token cost measurement alongside accuracy. The skill explicitly excludes general deployment without fine-tuning, agent creation, and prompt-only optimization, routing those to sibling azure-skills modules. Error handling documents API version issues, globalStandard training types, RFT endpoint scaling, deployment race conditions, and con.
highlights: Supports SFT, DPO, and RFT fine-tuning with dataset prep, training, deployment, and evaluation pipelines.
Ships Python scripts for submit, monitor, calibrate_grader, check_training, deploy, evaluate, and cleanup.
